issues.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is genuine and freely executed when the evidence supporting its execution is credible and the circumstances raised against it do not undermine that evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court found the will genuine and freely executed.
An advocate testified that he advised on preparation of the will and saw the testator sign it; the scribe testified that he prepared and explained it to the testator.
The scribe had recorded the gist of the will in a regularly kept register on the date it was said to have been executed, and that entry was not challenged.
The testator’s son did not deny that the signature on the will was his father’s.
The Court found no substance in the claims that the will was antedated, unnatural, or inconsistent with an undertaking in earlier proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings that the will was genuine and executed by the testator of his own free will were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the evidence of the advocate and scribe, the contemporaneous record of the will, the absence of a denial of the signature by the testator’s son, and the lack of substance in the circumstances said to discredit the will. It found no basis to disturb the concurrent factual findings of the courts below.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_concurrent_will_finding and (credible_execution_witnesses and contemporaneous_will_record) and signature_not_denied_by_close_relative

predicates.appeal_challenges_concurrent_will_findin: An appeal challenges concurrent findings by lower courts that a will was genuine and freely executed.
predicates.credible_execution_witnesses: A credible witness saw the testator sign the will, and a credible scribe testified that the will was prepared and explained to the testator.
predicates.contemporaneous_will_record: The scribe made a contemporaneous record of the substance of the will in a regularly kept register.
predicates.signature_not_denied_by_close_relative: A close relative who could address the testator’s signature did not deny that the signature on the will was the testator’s.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges concurrent findings about a will and the stated execution evidence is supported by a contemporaneous record and an un-denied signature, the will is treated as genuine and freely executed.

issues.legal_issue: Income earned by personally practising a hereditary profession is not, for that reason alone, joint family property.
material_facts: The testator practised a hereditary priestly profession and also held paid positions in the Maharaja’s service.
The evidence described payments from patrons as discretionary charity or remuneration for personal services, rather than sums claimable as of right.
The dispute concerned whether income from the hereditary profession was joint family property.
issues.conclusion: Income from the practice of the hereditary profession was not joint family property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court approved Hanso Pathak v. Harmandil Pathak, AIR 1934 Allahabad 851, which treated discretionary payments for charity or personal services as not claimable as of right and not family property, and as income acquired through learning. It overruled Chalabhai Gaurishankar v. Hargowan Ramji, I.L.R. 36 Bom. 94, insofar as it supported the contrary contention.

predicates.appeal_in_joint_family_property_dispute: An appeal in a property dispute concerns whether earnings belong to a joint family.
predicates.income_earned_from_personal_hereditary_p: A person earned income by personally practising a hereditary profession.

issues.definition: When a joint-family property dispute concerns income earned by a person practising a hereditary profession, that income is not treated as joint family property merely because the profession is hereditary.

issues.legal_issue: Property acquired by an individual from personal earnings is self-acquired when there is no evidence that ancestral family assets funded the acquisition.
material_facts: The testator received a salary and remuneration for service to the Maharaja in addition to income from his profession.
The evidence showed that the Maharaja gave land and constructed a building before giving it to the testator.
There was no evidence that family jewels or cash were used to acquire the property, and there was hardly any evidence of an ancestral nucleus.
The lower courts found the property to be the testator’s self-acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the property in item 1(a) was the testator’s self-acquired property was confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that earnings from practising a hereditary profession were not joint family property and relied on the testator’s means and the absence of evidence that an ancestral nucleus was used to acquire the property.

predicates.appeal_disputes_property_character: An appeal disputes whether property is an individual’s separate property or joint family property.
predicates.individual_had_personal_means: The individual had personal earnings or other means capable of funding the acquisition.
predicates.no_evidence_ancestral_assets_funded_acqu: There is no evidence that ancestral family assets were used to fund the acquisition.

issues.definition: When property is disputed in an appeal, the individual had personal means, and no ancestral funding is shown, the property is treated as self-acquired.

issues.legal_issue: A male Hindu may dispose of his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will where the applicable succession law deems that interest capable of testamentary disposition.
material_facts: The High Court found that two items of property were joint family property.
The parties accepted that the applicable succession law permitted a coparcener’s interest in joint family property to be disposed of by will.
The will was found genuine and freely executed.

The High Court awarded the beneficiary one-half of the two joint-family items on the basis that the family consisted of the testator and his son; the Supreme Court held that the beneficiary was entitled to at least one-third, with the testator’s precise interest to be determined on remand.
issues.conclusion: The testator could dispose of his interest in the joint family property by will; the beneficiary’s entitlement to one-third was decreed, and the extent of any greater bequeathable interest was remitted for determination.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Jammu and Kashmir Hindu Succession Act, 1956 provides that a Hindu may dispose by will of property capable of being disposed of by him in law. Its explanation deems a male Hindu’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property capable of disposition under the section.

predicates.appeal_concerns_bequest_of_joint_family_: An appeal concerns a will purporting to dispose of an interest in joint family property.
predicates.valid_will: The will was found genuine and freely executed.
predicates.testator_had_interest_in_mitakshara_copa: The testator held an interest in property belonging to a Mitakshara coparcenary.

issues.definition: When a valid will in an appeal concerns a testator’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property, the testator can bequeath that interest.

issues.legal_issue: The extent of a father’s interest in joint family property cannot be fixed without considering the mother’s entitlement on partition under the applicable Mitakshara law.
material_facts: The joint family property consisted of two items, and the testator’s son, wife, and granddaughter were among the parties claiming interests.
The High Court treated the joint family as consisting only of the testator and his son and awarded the beneficiary one-half under the will.
In an earlier partition suit, the son had claimed one-third, conceding that his father and mother were entitled to the other two-thirds.

The Supreme Court observed that under Mitakshara law, except in Madras, a mother is entitled to a share equal to a son when partition takes place between father and son, but no decision establishing the applicable position in Jammu and Kashmir had been cited.
The question of the testator’s precise interest had not been raised before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The question of the testator’s interest in the joint family property, and therefore the extent that could pass under the will, was remitted to the High Court for determination.
issues.legal_principle: The Court referred to Mulla’s Hindu Law and Mayne’s Hindu Law on a mother’s entitlement to a share equal to a son when partition occurs between father and son, and approved Dular Koeri v. Dwarkanath Misser, I.L.R. 32 Cal. 234; Sumrun Thakoor v. Chunder Mun Misser, I.L.R. 8 Cal. 17; Hosbanna Devanna Naik v. Devanna Sannappa Naik, I.L.R. 48 Bom. 468; and Pratap Singh v. Dalip Singh, I.L.R. 52 All. 596. Because the applicable law in Jammu and Kashmir had not been settled in the cited decisions, and the issue was a pure question of law relevant to the testator’s bequeathable interest, the Court remitted it to the High Court.

predicates.appeal_concerns_testator_interest_in_joi: An appeal concerns the extent of a deceased person’s interest in joint family property that was purportedly bequeathed.
predicates.mother_is_member_of_family: The deceased’s mother or wife is a member of the family whose interests in the property are in issue.
predicates.applicable_regional_rule_on_mothers_shar: The applicable regional law on the mother’s entitlement to a share when father and son partition has not been settled by a cited decision.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a deceased person’s joint-family interest, a mother’s share may affect that interest, and the applicable regional rule is unsettled, the High Court must determine the deceased person’s interest.
